result: Background claims establish that three opioid receptor subtypes (MOR, DOR, KOR) exist with unique distributions, and that existing fluorescent ligands have limitations due to decreased affinity and selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Kieffer and Evans 2009; Archer et al. 1992; Gaudriault et al. 1997; Madsen et al. 2000; Arttamangkul et al. 2000; Lam et al. 2018) and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

result: β-naltrexamine was selected as the guide molecule for NAI synthesis based on its high binding affinity for all opioid receptor subtypes, prior use in fluorescent conjugation with minimal affinity reduction, and relationship to β-FNA. The NAI linker was designed to be longer than β-FNA and to avoid the K233 attachment site.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are supported by citations (Emmerson et al. 1997; Portoghese et al. 1980) and established knowledge. Claims C8 and C54 describe rational design decisions supported by structural analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The design rationale is clearly articulated and justified.

result: NAI-A594 binds to MOR, DOR, and KOR with Ki values of approximately 50, 70, and 200 nM respectively, as determined by competitive radioligand binding assays.
evaluation: Claim C7 is based on only n=2 experiments of triplicate samples, which is insufficient for robust statistical characterization. The reported Ki values lack error estimates and the sample size is too small to assess variability. Additional replicates are needed to confidently establish binding affinities.

result: NAI-A594 labeling of FMOR-expressing HEK293 cells is stable after naloxone wash, in contrast to the reversible ligand NTX-A594. Flow cytometry shows NAI-A594 labeling intensity similar to antibody labeling, with 30% reduction after naloxone wash and 98% reduction when naloxone is co-incubated during labeling.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C13-C15, C58-C59, and C73 are supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches (confocal microscopy Figure 2A, flow cytometry Figure 2B) with appropriate controls (naloxone wash, NTX-A594 comparison, co-incubation). The data consistently demonstrate covalent labeling with a reversible component. Sample sizes are stated (n=3) and results are internally consistent.

result: NAI-A594 labeling of FDOR-expressing cells was comparable to FMOR after naloxone wash, while persistent labeling of FKOR was negligible.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with stated sample sizes (n=3-5). The differential labeling of receptor subtypes is consistent with the binding affinities reported in C7 and provides important selectivity information.

result: Western blot analysis with anti-A488 antibody detected a ~75 kDa FMOR band only in cells labeled with NAI-A488 in the absence of naloxone, confirming irreversible binding. Purified FMOR co-incubated with naloxone showed no significant fluorescence.
evaluation: Claims C16 and C60 are supported by immunoprecipitation-Western blot data (Figure 2C) and in-gel fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) with appropriate controls (naloxone co-incubation, unlabeled cells, HEK293 without FMOR). The experiments were repeated twice, providing biochemical confirmation of covalent labeling.

result: Time-course analysis showed that attachment of A488 to purified FMOR increased with time and reached maximal intensity after 48 hours.
evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by in-gel fluorescence data (Figure 2E) from two independent experiments. The time course provides important kinetic information about the labeling reaction, though the slow kinetics at room temperature is noted as potentially due to temperature and receptor conformation.

result: NAI-A594 labeled FMORs co-localized with M1-A488 in the cytoplasm after agonist-induced internalization in HEK293 cells.
evaluation: Claim C18 is supported by confocal imaging data (Figure 2F) showing co-localization of both labels in endosomes after ME application. This demonstrates that labeled receptors retain the ability to bind agonist and internalize, an important functional validation.

result: NAI-A594 labeled endogenous MORs in LC neurons of brain slices with stable fluorescence after naloxone wash (40% decrease in intensity). NTX-A594 labeling was inefficient and nearly abolished after ACSF wash. No labeling was observed in MOR knockout rats, and labeling was blocked by CTAP in THGFP mice.
evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by multiple imaging modalities (macroscopic, 2-photon microscopy) with appropriate controls (naloxone wash, NTX-A594 comparison, MOR-KO rats, CTAP blockade). The convergent evidence from different controls strongly supports MOR-specific labeling in native tissue. Sample sizes and quantification are provided (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

result: NAI-A594 labeled neurons in the lateral parabrachial nucleus and hippocampal formation, with fluorescent patterns in hippocampus similar to MOR-specific immunohistochemistry in fixed tissue.
evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by macroscopic and microscopic imaging data (Figure 3A, 3C) and comparison to prior immunohistochemistry (Arvidsson et al. 1995a). The consistency with established MOR distribution patterns provides validation of the labeling specificity.

result: NAI-A594 labeling of endogenous MORs in brain slices was concentration-dependent (detectable at 10 nM, well-defined at 100 nM) and time-dependent (increasing from 0.5 to 2 hours), with no additional increase beyond 2 hours.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29, C61-C62 are supported by systematic concentration and time-course experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) with stated sample sizes (3-7 slices, 3-4 rats). The dose-response and kinetic characterization is important for establishing optimal labeling conditions.

result: NAI-A594 labeled FMORs deep in brain slices (90 μm) where M1-A488 antibody labeling was not well-defined, demonstrating superior tissue penetration.
evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by 2-photon microscopy z-stack imaging (Figure 3D, Videos 1-4) with quantification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). The comparison to antibody labeling demonstrates a key advantage of the small molecule approach for deep tissue imaging.

result: NAI-A594 revealed distinct fluorescent patches in mouse striatum consistent with MOR distribution in striosomes, which was blocked by CTAP. This pattern is consistent with known MOR localization in patches versus diffuse DOR/KOR distribution.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by imaging data (Figure 4) with CTAP blockade control. Claims C63-C65 provide context from prior literature (Arvidsson et al. 1995b; Miura et al. 2007; Banghart et al. 2015). The patch pattern is consistent with known MOR distribution and provides strong evidence for MOR selectivity in native tissue.

result: NAI-A594 did not efficiently label endogenous DORs in cortical brain slices despite known DOR immunoreactivity in this region.
evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by experimental observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) and comparison to prior immunohistochemistry (Cahill et al. 2001). This unexpected finding is important for understanding the selectivity of NAI-A594 and is discussed in relation to potential mechanisms (C45-C47).

result: Strong NAI-A594 fluorescence was found in thalamus and habenula, which was absent in MOR knockout rats.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by imaging data (Figure 5) with MOR-KO control. The knockout control provides strong evidence for MOR specificity of labeling in these brain regions.

result: Only ~3% of THGFP-positive dopamine neurons in midbrain showed NAI-A594 labeling, but extensive labeling of processes was observed and blocked by naloxone and CTAP. This is consistent with known KOR expression in most dopamine neurons and MOR expression in a small subset.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by quantitative imaging data (Figure 6A: 3/90 cells, 8 slices, 3 animals) with antagonist blockade controls (Figure 6B). Claims C67-C68 provide literature context (Arvidsson et al. 1995b; Ford et al. 2006, 2007). The low percentage of labeled cell bodies with extensive process labeling suggests MOR-positive inputs to the midbrain.

result: NAI-A594 (500 nM) acts as a reversible antagonist, decreasing ME-activated GIRK current by approximately half during 5-minute application, with recovery after washout. Lower concentrations (30-100 nM) showed less than 10% inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C37 and C69 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 7A) demonstrating reversible antagonism. The concentration-dependence is important for establishing that labeling concentrations (30-100 nM) have minimal functional effects. The reversibility after washout is consistent with the traceless labeling mechanism.

result: LC neurons labeled with NAI-A594 (30 nM, 1 hour) showed no difference in ME-induced current amplitude compared to untreated cells.
evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 7B-b) with citations to prior work establishing normal response ranges (Osborne and Williams 1995; Levitt and Williams 2012; Arttamangkul et al. 2018). This is a critical functional validation showing that labeled receptors retain normal agonist responsiveness.

result: After ME application, NAI-A594 fluorescence decreased along the plasma membrane without clear cytoplasmic puncta, while M1-A488 labeled receptors showed clear internalized puncta. Similar 30-40% fluorescence decreases occurred with ME, morphine, or naloxone application.
evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C72 are supported by 2-photon microscopy data (Figure 7C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The differential behavior of NAI-A594 versus M1-A488 after agonist application is well-documented. However, the mechanism for fluorescence decrease remains unclear, and the authors appropriately discuss potential explanations (quenching ruled out by C71, competitive binding suggested by C73).

result: NAI-A594 can be used at low nanomolar concentrations (10-100 nM) or high concentration (500 nM for 5 min) to efficiently label endogenous MORs in brain slices, allowing visualization of opioid-sensitive neurons without loss of receptor function.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C74 are supported by the collective experimental data throughout the manuscript, including concentration-dependence studies (C28-C29), time-course studies (C28), rapid labeling (C43), and functional validation (C37-C38). The claims represent well-supported conclusions from the body of work.

result: MOR has 12 potentially reactive amino acids for NAI, while KOR has 8 and DOR only 3. The paucity of reactive amino acids in DOR and potentially lower DOR plasma membrane density may explain the selectivity for MOR over DOR in brain slices.
evaluation: Claim C45 is based on sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but the counting of 'potentially reactive' amino acids is not clearly defined or validated. Claims C46-C47 are speculative explanations (explicitly stated as 'may be') for the observed MOR selectivity. While plausible, these mechanisms are not directly tested and remain hypothetical. Additional experiments would be needed to validate these proposed mechanisms.

result: NAI-A594 is a valuable tool for studying MOR functionality and circuitry in living brain slices from wild-type animals, with advantages including simple labeling procedures, detection of endogenous receptors, and flexibility in experimental conditions.
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 and C75 represent conclusions about the utility and impact of the developed method. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental validation throughout the manuscript, including demonstrations in multiple brain regions, functional validation, and comparison to existing methods. The claims appropriately summarize the significance of the work.

result: The traceless affinity labeling approach uses a high-affinity ligand to direct probe binding near the ligand binding site, with close proximity enabling use of mild reactivity probes. The acylimidazole reactive group can react with Lys, Ser, Tyr, and Thr residues, and after transfer the dye remains attached while the ligand dissociates.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C55-C56 describe the established principles and prior applications of traceless affinity labeling, supported by citations to the relevant literature (Fujishima et al. 2012; Yamaura et al. 2016; Wakayama et al. 2017). These provide appropriate background and context for the current work.

result: The weak antagonism of NAI-A594 is likely due to the bulky Alexa594 moiety, as NAI-AK without the dye significantly blocks MOR at 300 nM. Fluorescence quenching in acidic endosomes can be ruled out because A594 is pH insensitive.
evaluation: Claim C70 is a reasonable inference supported by experimental comparison of NAI-A594 versus NAI-AK (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), though explicitly stated as speculative ('probably due to'). Claim C71 is supported by citation to dye properties (Panchuk-Voloshina et al. 1999). Both claims appropriately address potential concerns about the labeling approach.
